title: Microservices Pattern: Pattern: Saga
snippet: A saga is a sequence of local transactions where each local transaction updates the database and publishes a message or event to trigger the next local transaction in the saga. The Saga pattern provides a practical approach to distributed transactions in microservices architectures, trading strict ACID guarantees for better availability and scalability by decomposing transactions into local operations with compensating actions.

title: Understanding Compensation Transactions in the Saga Pattern - A Comprehensive Guide
snippet: A compensating transaction is a new operation that is the logical inverse of the one it undoes. If any step fails, the saga executes compensating transactions to undo the changes made by preceding steps. Every step that can fail must have a well-tested compensating transaction.

title: Event Sourcing: compensation – the simple way out when things go wrong
snippet: The system doesn't update existing data in an event sourcing store. Instead, it adds new entries that transition the state of entities to the new values. Compensation can be used to avoid relying on a distributed transaction coordinator and to introduce no technical dependency (the transaction) between subsystems, since not all storage systems support transactions.

title: Saga Pattern in Microservices: A Mastery Guide | Temporal
snippet: Temporal.io stands out among orchestration and workflow engines like Camunda Zeebe and Netflix Conductor for being more developer-friendly with its code-based workflow approach and for natively supporting the execution of the Saga pattern through its Temporal-SDK Saga API.

title: Saga Orchestration vs Choreography | Temporal
snippet: In orchestration, a single orchestrator manages the transaction flow, invoking services and handling compensations when needed. In choreography, each service listens for events and independently triggers subsequent actions.

title: How to Implement the Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions
snippet: Idempotency is not optional—messages will be delivered more than once, and every participant must handle duplicates gracefully. Every step in a saga should have a timeout, and if a service does not respond within a defined period, the orchestrator should either retry or fail the step.
